title: Adab of the road
hook: the companions want to keep sitting by the road, so they're told what the road is owed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of knowledge, and your line: learn, then do. What did you do with the one thing you chose? Today we step out the front door and onto the street. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

Do roads have rights? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says they do. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reports that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told his companions to avoid sitting along the roads. They pushed back. Those are our meeting places, they said. That's where we talk. We can't help it. So he didn't argue. He said, in paraphrase: if you must sit there, then give the road its right. And they asked the obvious next question. What is the road's right?
screen: `DO ROADS HAVE RIGHTS?` → `WE CAN'T HELP SITTING THERE.` → `THEN GIVE THE ROAD ITS RIGHT.`

segments.voice: His answer, in paraphrase: lowering the gaze, holding back harm, returning the greeting, and urging what is good while forbidding what is wrong. Notice the shape. A street belongs to no one in particular, and that doesn't make it a free-for-all. Everyone on it is owed something by everyone else. First, the eyes. The Qur'an says it in surah al-Nur, in Pickthall's translation: "Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and be modest." The next verse says the same to the believing women. On a crowded street, lowering the gaze is a kind of privacy you give people who can't close a door. Second, harm. Bukhari tells of a man walking along a road who found a thorny branch lying across it and moved it aside, and Allah thanked him for it and forgave him. That's the whole story. One branch. And in Sahih Muslim, faith is described as having many branches, the highest being the declaration that there is no god but Allah, and the lowest, removing something harmful from the road. Even the lowest branch is still faith. Third, the greeting. Al-Nisa, Pickthall again: "When ye are greeted with a greeting, greet ye with a better than it or return it." A greeting on the street isn't a favor you can skip. It's owed back, and better if you can. And the last piece turns the sidewalk into a place where people look out for one another. The companions asked for permission to sit. What they got was a job.
screen: `A STREET OWES, AND IS OWED.` · `LOWER THE GAZE.` · `MOVE THE THORNY BRANCH.` · `RETURN THE GREETING, OR BETTER.`

segments.voice: The practice: give the road its rights. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the street, hallway or parking lot you'll pass through next. See the people on it. Where would your eyes wander that they don't need to? Let them come down, gently. What's lying in the way that you could move: a bottle, a cart, a bag in the aisle? See your hand moving it. Who might greet you? Hear yourself answering, a little warmer than they did. If you pray, you can return a salam with wa 'alaykum al-salam. The bell holds the time.
Adab of the road. The manners of shared space: lower the gaze, hold back harm and clear it away, return the greeting, and urge the good. Today's word.

Your line: the road's rights. Today, move one thing out of someone's way, and return one greeting a little better than it came. Tomorrow, the adab of the market. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims cite the hadith of the road's rights when teaching public manners, and treat lowering the gaze, returning salam and removing harm from the path as acts of faith.

pairs: the road's right for the eyes
moved aside, and the man forgiven

myth: the companions were simply forbidden to sit by the road
when they said they had no choice, he said: then give the road its right.
returning a greeting with a better one is in the Qur'an
al-Nisa: greet ye with a better than it or return it.
removing harm from the road is counted as a branch of faith
in Sahih Muslim, the lowest branch of faith is removing something harmful from the road.

fork.setup: you're walking along a road and a thorny branch lies across it. nobody's watching. what does the man in the hadith do?
options: step around it; someone else will move it.
move it out of the way.
complain about it to the first person he meets.
fork.reveal: he moved the branch aside, and the hadith says Allah thanked him for it and forgave him. one branch.

original.note: Arabic: a right, a due; the road's haqq.

trapdoor: what you thought: the adab of the road is traffic manners.
what it means: shared space has a claim on everyone in it: eyes lowered, harm cleared away, greetings returned, good encouraged.
what a scholar hears: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri's hadith on the road's haqq, beside Muslim's report that removing harm from the road is a branch of faith.
